quiz.title: Unit 9 SAQ 02
quiz.headline: AIDS in Africa
quiz.prompt: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question.
quiz.instructions: Answer all three parts. For each part, Answer the question directly, Prove it with specific historical evidence, and Explain how the evidence supports your answer. On the AP exam each part earns one point. This is self-assessment practice, not official College Board scoring.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice in AP short-answer format. Model answers show one strong response; other accurate, well-supported answers can earn the point.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: George W. Bush, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 28, 2003
stimulusBlocks.citation: George W. Bush, Address Before a Joint Session of the Congress on the State of the Union, January 28, 2003. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/2003-GWBush.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: Anti-retroviral drugs slow the HIV virus and extend the lives of people with AIDS. Bush proposed the program that became the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR).
stimulusBlocks.text:
Today, on the continent of Africa, nearly 30 million people have the AIDS virus - including three million children under the age of 15. There are whole countries in Africa where more than one-third of the adult population carries the infection. More than four million require immediate drug treatment. Yet across that continent, only 50,000 AIDS victims - only 50,000 - are receiving the medicine they need. . . .

AIDS can be prevented. Anti-retroviral drugs can extend life for many years. And the cost of those drugs has dropped from 12,000 dollars a year to under 300 dollars a year - which places a tremendous possibility within our grasp. . . .

I ask the Congress to commit 15 billion dollars over the next five years, including nearly ten billion dollars in new money, to turn the tide against AIDS in the most afflicted nations of Africa and the Caribbean.

scaffold.label: Answer
scaffold.text: Respond directly to the task verb: identify, describe, or explain.

scaffold.label: Prove
scaffold.text: Name a specific person, place, institution, or development.

scaffold.label: Explain
scaffold.text: Show how or why the evidence answers the question.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE reason George W. Bush gives for why action against AIDS in Africa was possible in 2003.
criteria: States a specific reason from the passage.
Connects the reason to the possibility of treatment or prevention.

model.answer: Bush says the cost of anti-retroviral drugs had fallen sharply.
model.prove: He notes that the drugs that cost 12,000 dollars a year now cost under 300 dollars, and that AIDS can be prevented.
model.explain: Lower prices made it realistic for governments to treat millions of people, so a large aid program could save many lives.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify his statement that anti-retroviral drugs can extend life for many years.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way globalization in the second half of the twentieth century contributed to the spread of disease.
criteria: Names a specific development, such as travel, migration, or urbanization.
Explains how it helped a disease spread.

model.answer: Faster and cheaper travel allowed diseases to move across regions quickly.
model.prove: Jet air travel after the 1950s carried millions of passengers across continents, and migration from rural areas to crowded cities increased contact among people.
model.explain: Infected people could reach distant places in hours, before symptoms appeared, so epidemics spread more widely than they could when travel took weeks.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain how growing cities in Africa, Asia, and Latin America created conditions in which diseases such as HIV and cholera spread.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way medical advances or international cooperation reduced the impact of a disease in the twentieth century.
criteria: Names a specific disease and a specific advance or program.
Explains how it reduced the disease's effects.

model.answer: A global vaccination campaign eliminated smallpox.
model.prove: The World Health Organization led an international campaign of vaccination and tracking of cases that ended with the declaration in 1980 that smallpox had been eradicated.
model.explain: Cooperation among governments allowed vaccination teams to reach remote areas, showing that organized international action could defeat a disease that had killed millions.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain the development of antibiotics such as penicillin, the polio vaccines of the 1950s, or antiretroviral treatment for HIV.
